newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian court frees E. Timor activists.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian court frees E. Timor activists.

text.p: A Malaysian High Court on Thursday ordered the immediate release from jail of the last 10 human rights activists detained after last weekend's disruption of an East Timor conference by a pro-government youth mob.
The 10 walked out of a police lock-up in Kuala Lumpur into the arms of supporters and relatives, all shouting "Viva East Timor", the territory Indonesia invaded in 1975 and annexed the next year.
"This is, without doubt, the most successful conference on East Timor," said one of the 10, lawyer R. Sivarasa, after a spokesman for the activists read out a joint statement condemning their arrest.
"We had an agenda for the conference but in terms of media coverage we got the best in the world for East Timor."

The Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor II (APCET II) was broken up on Saturday soon after it started, when youths allied to the government smashed into the meeting at a Kuala Lumpur hotel, overturning furniture and manhandling delegates.

Police detained more than 100 conference participants, journalists and protesters. Police released the protesters on Saturday. The 46 foreign participants were deported. All but 10 of the activists had been released earlier this week.

On Wednesday, the Kuala Lumpur High Court overturned a Magistrates Court order that would have kept the 10 activists in jail until Saturday to allow police to investigate whether to bring charges against them and to identify ringleaders.
"The detention is illegal as at now and they should be released immediately and not held another second," High Court Judge V.C. Vohrah said in his order.
He said the police had not specified in their request why the detainees had been arrested in the first place and why they needed to be detained longer.
APCET II aimed to focus international attention on East Timor, whose annexation by Indonesia has never been recognised by the United Nations.
The conference was held ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili.
The Malaysian government had objected to the conference, saying it could harm ties with neighbouring Indonesia, but stopped short of outrightly banning it.

The chairman of the youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) party on Thursday defended the storming of the conference, saying the youths had to act to protect their government's credibility.

"It is clear and blatant that the non-governmental organisations involved (in the conference) were least concerned or bothered about the government's stand," Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, UMNO youth chief, told a news conference.

A joint statement by the detainees, read by human rights activist Kua Kia Soong, said: "Through this dastardly affair, the Malaysian government has exposed its own double standards on human rights in the world.

"We the Malaysian NGOs (non-governmental organisations) who are concerned to find a path to peace in East Timor are merely trying to practise what the prime minister preaches about defending human rights in South Africa, Palestine, Bosnia and elsewhere."
